pos: proper n. (the eastern limit of the Persian empire)
etymology: Hebrew hoddu, from the Old Persian Hindu, the land of the river Indus (Sanskrit Sindhu, river). In Esther it means the Indus region, the eastern frontier of Persia, not the whole subcontinent.
biblical_def: India appears only in Esther, as one end of a king's reach. “Now it came to pass in the days of Ahasuerus, (this is Ahasuerus which reigned, from India even unto Ethiopia, over an hundred and seven and twenty provinces:)” (Esther 1:1). When Mordecai's counter-decree went out, it went the same distance: “and to the lieutenants, and the deputies and rulers of the provinces which are from India unto Ethiopia” (Esther 8:9). The phrase measures the greatest empire the world had yet seen, and the book uses it to show how far one Persian decree could reach to destroy the Jews, and how far God could send the decree that saved them. A greater dominion was promised to David's Son: “He shall have dominion also from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth” (Psalm 72:8). Ahasuerus ruled from India to Ethiopia; Christ rules all nations, and His gospel has gone to India and beyond.

pos: proper n. (the Roman provinces of the Iberian peninsula, Paul’s intended field)
etymology: Greek Spania, Latin Hispania, the Roman name of the Iberian peninsula; perhaps of Phoenician origin.
biblical_def: Spain was the horizon of Paul's ambition. He wrote to Rome from Corinth, having preached from Jerusalem round about to Illyricum, and he explained the principle that drove him: “Yea, so have I strived to preach the gospel, not where Christ was named, lest I should build upon another man's foundation” (Romans 15:20). Rome was not his goal but his base: “Whensoever I take my journey into Spain, I will come to you: for I trust to see you in my journey, and to be brought on my way thitherward by you” (Romans 15:24). He repeated the plan after the collection for Jerusalem: “When therefore I have performed this, and have sealed to them this fruit, I will come by you into Spain” (Romans 15:28). Paul reached Rome in chains rather than on his own schedule. Whether he afterward reached Spain Scripture does not say, though Clement of Rome wrote that he came to the limit of the west. Spain stands as the mark of a man who measured his work by the places Christ was not yet named.

pos: proper n. (Roman region on the eastern Adriatic, part of Illyricum)
etymology: Greek Dalmatia, from the Dalmatae, an Illyrian people of the eastern shore of the Adriatic.
biblical_def: Dalmatia is named in Paul's last letter, in a list of comings and goings that reads like a war report. “For Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world, and is departed unto Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, Titus unto Dalmatia” (2 Timothy 4:10). The verse sets two departures side by side. Demas left because he loved the present world; Titus went because the work required him. Dalmatia lay within Illyricum, the region Paul had reached years earlier: “so that from Jerusalem, and round about unto Illyricum, I have fully preached the gospel of Christ” (Romans 15:19). From his last prison the old apostle was still deploying men to the field. His next words are a request and a reconciliation: “Only Luke is with me. Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry” (2 Timothy 4:11).

pos: proper n. (region northeast of Galilee, part of Philip’s tetrarchy)
etymology: Greek Itouraia, the land of the Ituraeans, an Arab people of the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon, commonly traced to Jetur the son of Ishmael.
biblical_def: Ituraea is named once, in Luke's great dating sentence: “Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judaea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituraea and of the region of Trachonitis, and Lysanias the tetrarch of Abilene” (Luke 3:1). The Philip named here is Herod the Great's son, ruler of the lands northeast of the Sea of Galilee, who rebuilt Caesarea Philippi. The Ituraeans are commonly traced back to the Ishmaelite tribe of Jetur, named among Ishmael's sons: “Hadar, and Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah” (Genesis 25:15). Israel's tribes beyond Jordan once fought them: “And they made war with the Hagarites, with Jetur, and Nephish, and Nodab” (1 Chronicles 5:19). So Luke's list of rulers quietly gathers the descendants of Ishmael into the setting of the gospel's first preaching.

pos: proper n. (tetrarchy of Lysanias, northwest of Damascus)
etymology: Greek Abilene, the district of Abila, a town in the Anti-Lebanon on the road from Damascus to Heliopolis.
biblical_def: Abilene is named once, as the last item in Luke's list of rulers: “and Lysanias the tetrarch of Abilene” (Luke 3:1). The district took its name from Abila, a town in the mountains northwest of Damascus, and an inscription from that town names a Lysanias as tetrarch in the reign of Tiberius, exactly as Luke says. Luke had promised such care at the opening of his Gospel: “It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus” (Luke 1:3), “That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed” (Luke 1:4). Every name in the list is there for the sake of that certainty. The gospel did not begin in a timeless myth but in a particular year, under particular rulers, when “the word of God came unto John the son of Zacharias in the wilderness” (Luke 3:2).

pos: proper n. (the sea in which Paul’s ship was driven)
etymology: Greek Adrias, from the town of Adria near the mouth of the Po; in the first century the name covered not only the modern Adriatic but the central Mediterranean between Crete, Sicily and Greece.
biblical_def: Paul's ship drifted for two weeks in the sea called Adria. Luke recorded the despair aboard: “And when neither sun nor stars in many days appeared, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope that we should be saved was then taken away” (Acts 27:20). Then land came near: “But when the fourteenth night was come, as we were driven up and down in Adria, about midnight the shipmen deemed that they drew near to some country” (Acts 27:27). The sailors sounded and found twenty fathoms, then fifteen; Paul had already told them that an angel had promised every life. The promise held exactly: “And the rest, some on boards, and some on broken pieces of the ship. And so it came to pass, that they escaped all safe to land” (Acts 27:44). Two hundred seventy-six souls were driven up and down in Adria, and not one was lost, because God had said so.

pos: n. (the tempestuous northeast wind that drove Paul’s ship)
etymology: Greek euroklydon, as read in the Received Text, from Euros, the east wind, and klydon, a wave, surge; a sailors' name for a violent northeasterly gale.
biblical_def: The voyage had begun gently. “And when the south wind blew softly, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, loosing thence, they sailed close by Crete” (Acts 27:13). Then the weather turned: “But not long after there arose against it a tempestuous wind, called Euroclydon” (Acts 27:14). The ship could not face it: “And when the ship was caught, and could not bear up into the wind, we let her drive” (Acts 27:15). Paul had warned against sailing; the centurion had believed the master of the ship instead. Yet in the middle of the gale it was Paul who stood up with a word from God: “Wherefore, sirs, be of good cheer: for I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me” (Acts 27:25). Euroclydon was the strongest wind the Mediterranean could throw at a grain ship, and it drove Paul exactly where God meant him to go.

etymology: From wind, Old English wind, plus the adjective suffix -y, Old English -ig: full of wind.
biblical_def: David wrote Psalm 55 when betrayal came from his own household, and his first instinct was flight. “And I said, Oh that I had wings like a dove! for then would I fly away, and be at rest” (Psalm 55:6). He would lodge in the wilderness: “I would hasten my escape from the windy storm and tempest” (Psalm 55:8). The windy storm is the violence and strife in the city, and the treachery of a familiar friend. But the psalm does not end in flight. David turns from wishing for wings to casting his load on God, and leaves the counsel to all who are in the same wind: “Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved” (Psalm 55:22). The windy storm cannot be outrun by dove's wings, but the believer can be held fast in it.

etymology: From rain, Old English regn, plus the adjective suffix -y: abounding with rain.
biblical_def: Proverbs uses the rainy day for one of its sharpest household portraits. “A continual dropping in a very rainy day and a contentious woman are alike” (Proverbs 27:15). In a house of beaten earth and timber, a long rain found every weakness in the roof, and the drip did not stop. The next verse adds that she cannot be restrained: “Whosoever hideth her hideth the wind, and the ointment of his right hand, which bewrayeth itself” (Proverbs 27:16). The same picture appears earlier: “A foolish son is the calamity of his father: and the contentions of a wife are a continual dropping” (Proverbs 19:13). The proverb does not despise women; the same book closes with the virtuous woman whose price is far above rubies. It warns against a particular sin, contention, which wears a household down not by storm but by the steady drip of the rainy day.

corruption_paragraphs: Critics read the contentious-woman proverbs as evidence of a patriarchal contempt for women. Proverbs is equally severe on the angry man, the sluggard, the fool and the talebearer, and it ends with the highest praise of a wife in all ancient literature.

The principle to recover is the peace of a godly household under the creational order Scripture gives it. A gentle and quiet spirit is of great price in the sight of God, and contention, from husband or wife, is the continual dropping that rots a house.

etymology: From snow, Old English snaw, plus the adjective suffix -y.
biblical_def: The snowy day belongs to one of David's mighty men. “Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, the son of a valiant man of Kabzeel, who had done many acts; he slew two lionlike men of Moab: also he went down and slew a lion in a pit in a snowy day” (1 Chronicles 11:22). Every detail is against him: a lion, trapped and therefore desperate; a pit, with no room to escape; snow, slick footing and numb hands. Benaiah went down anyway. The righteous courage the proverb praises is exactly this: “The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion” (Proverbs 28:1). And the snow itself is God's: “He giveth snow like wool: he scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes” (Psalm 147:16). The man who served the God of the snow did not fear the snowy day, and Benaiah rose to command Solomon's army.
